samples.visibleText: 1 2 3 4 5 ADA MENSAH FIRMWARE / MOSSLINK LOCAL PROTOTYPE · FICTIONAL 1 / Code → check How do you check a decision made in code? Ada Mensah works with embedded firmware: code that controls a physical device. For Mosslink, an environmental sensor, she wrote the firmware, scheduled power states and built the bring-up fixture. Bring-up means checking a new board’s basic operation. Follow the connection from a code decision to something observable on the bench. Fictional prototype · The apparatus is an explanatory model, not an actual Mosslink device.

targets.html:
3 / Bring-up

A command needs a physical check.

Firmware sends a command; the board responds. The bring-up fixture provides access so that behavior on the physical board can be checked through a bench observation. The fixture supports inspection; it does not replace the board’s circuitry.

Ada wrote the firmware, scheduled power states and built the fixture. A colleague designed the PCB (printed circuit board) and the analogue front end, the circuitry handling analogue signals.

The separated rig illustrates those relationships. It is not a circuit, wiring plan or recovered implementation.

targets.html:
4 / Evidence

Two paths. Two different claims.

Measured sleep and transmit current, together with an assumed reporting interval, support a two-year projection. A separate continuous bench run supports 72 hours observed.

The 72-hour run does not validate two years of endurance. Neither path establishes field conditions or customer deployment. State tables, timing diagrams, current traces and bench checklists are working documents; no original measurement table, trace, spreadsheet or run notebook is supplied here.
